title: Project 1 opens, my first p5.js sketch, Boyd's feedback, and my first server
introduction: There were four lessons this week. On Tuesday, Boyd launched the new unit on ‘Communication Technologies’ and introduced ‘Project 1’. ‘Project 0’ was a broadcast: I told a story, and you came along to experience it. ‘Project 1’, on the other hand, was a ‘duet’: two websites calling each other’s real-time data. On Wednesday, we joined Ross for our first p5.js workshop, where I built a small solar system from scratch in a blank editor. On Thursday, Boyd led the Project 1 workshop, and I presented my process prototype; his feedback is the most important part of this blog post. On Friday, Ross demonstrated how to run a Node.js server on our own laptops, which is one of the essential building blocks required for Project 1.
related_work:
The topic of Boyd’s lecture was ‘Data as the Cornerstone of the Web’. For every file, you need to ask two questions: Can a browser read it? How large is the file? Raster images write every pixel to the file, so the files

are large; vector images, on the other hand, consist of a set of instructions, so the files are smaller. He then shifted the discussion from content creation to content delivery. No data on the internet is transmitted in its entirety: it is all broken down into data packets. WebSocket maintains a continuous connection, whilst an intermediary server forwards data from Website 1 to Website 2. Project 1 is built precisely on the basis of this ‘intermediary server’ [1]. In Boyd’s demonstration, two people were driving a car together; the system did not transmit video, but only information regarding the positions the objects should occupy, making the transmission both lightweight and fast.

Ross once said something about learning that I wish to bear in mind: look at the official examples, copy some parts, modify others, and it becomes your own. Regarding artificial intelligence, his view is clear: you need a certain level of knowledge to engage in critical learning from AI [2].

On Thursday, Boyd mentioned that ‘Project 1’ could take four forms: a duet, a collective, a constellation or a cooperative game. Our project falls under the category of a duet. One phrase worth remembering is ‘the aesthetic experience of co-existence in separation’ [3]. I was particularly struck by the section on mirrors, which was based on Boyd’s own research. During video calls, we all find ourselves surreptitiously gazing at our own tiny windows. He asked us to switch on our front-facing cameras, and I became the demonstration subject: the moment I saw myself, I quickly smoothed my hair. In his ‘Virtual Director’ project, when people see themselves and others in a shared 3D space, they stop staring at their own faces and begin to interact [3].
method:
Wednesday. We began by learning about `createCanvas`, `background`, `circle`, `fill`, `mouseX`, `mouseY` and `frameCount`, followed by some free practice. My implementation sequence was as follows: first, I drew a sun in the centre; then I drew a planet with an x-coordinate of `sunX + cos(frameCount * 0.02) * 150`, whilst the y- coordinate was calculated using `sin` instead of `cos`; a second, slower-moving planet; a satellite centred on the

first planet, with coordinates calculated using the same formula as for the first planet; two orbital lines; 150 stars generated within a `for` loop, with `randomSeed` used to keep them in place; and a comet consisting of 12 circles that gradually become smaller and dimmer. This sketch has been published online [4]; The p5 pages I referred to included ‘Sine Cosine’, ‘Repeating with Loops’ and ‘Variables and Change’ [5].

Thursday. Boyd shared the server code for Project 1, and we ran a test of the sample project ‘CollideTogether’ [6]. To be honest, I didn’t quite grasp how to incorporate multiplayer interaction, so I spent most of the time playing on my own with those grey avatars. However, I did understand the underlying principle: there is a server in the middle that transmits only position data and a small amount of text, with no video stream. Afterwards, I showed Boyd my workflow prototype. The story centres on a man and a woman who grew up together but now live in different cities. Players must make one of four gestures (calm, smile, look down, surprise); they will then see a childhood silhouette of the other person displaying that emotion, accompanied by a line of text. After three rounds of interaction, the shared images are pieced together, and a ‘wall of memories’ comprising sixteen frames lights up.

Friday. To enable two computers to communicate, we needed an intermediary server, so we each set one up on our own laptops. Node.js was responsible for running the server, Express for serving the files in the public folder (my ‘Solar System’ project was running on localhost:3000), whilst socket.io maintained an open communication channel with each connected browser. It took just twenty-one lines of code in total [7]. The gesture side, ml5, comes next week.
results_discussion:
I spent most of Wednesday afternoon sorting out errors, and these errors proved even more instructive than the lines of code that ran without a hitch. The unquoted `fill(red)` still displayed black, because `red` without quotation marks is a non-existent variable. A missing closing brace in the `draw` statement caused an ‘unexpected end of input’ error. The two errors that taught me the most were both related to the orbits: the x- axis code used 0.02, whilst the y-axis code used 0.03, causing the planet to follow a strange trajectory; furthermore, my orbit code was defined as 300 × 180, forming an ellipse, so the planet could never remain within the orbit. These two lines of code must use the same speed and radius, and the orbit’s diameter must be twice the radius. What I now understand is this: `draw` runs sixty times per second; `frameCount` represents time; and the position of all moving objects is calculated by multiplying `frameCount` by the speed, then applying the cosine and sine functions. When I encountered difficulties, I sought help from the AI, but I typed every line of code myself, repeatedly trialling, making mistakes and correcting them until I truly understood how it worked.

Boyd’s feedback is the part I’m most keen to retain this week. He liked the concept: striving to communicate with others through gestures, and putting oneself in the other person’s shoes to imagine how they might be feeling. However, he raised some questions about the opening section. My interaction loop is closed, but the previous one was not. This project is built on the foundation of my partner and I knowing each other well. For two strangers standing in front of the screen, there is currently a lack of motivation: why would they reach out, what are they doing, and what do they gain from it? He referred to this as the ‘onboarding’. When I began to explain it from a technical perspective (sign language for four emotions), he interrupted me: that’s the technical aspect; we need the artistic dimension, the narrative dimension, and why it matters [3]. He gave two examples: one was ‘characterisation’ (the screen prompts you to reconstruct someone’s memories through gestures, one question per round, followed by the display of ‘Memory sent’ and ‘Memory received’); the other was ‘discovery’ (at a certain point, the visitor should realise that the other person is a real human being, not an AI). Thus, what was missing was not the code. Rather, it was that initial interface that gives a stranger a reason— one question per round, turning gestures into answers, and signalling that the other person is a real human being. This ‘mirror lecture’ also explained a choice I had made intuitively: users would never see their own faces on my screen, only a drawn silhouette.

The questions I raised last Friday, and my current understanding of them:

• Why isn’t the terminal updating? It never runs anything automatically; the code only runs when I type `node server.js`. First, save the file; when `server.js` changes, restart the server. If only the `public` directory has changed, simply refresh the page.

• Why did `npm install` output a long string of text whilst Ross’s screen remained static? Node is already installed on my laptop, so npm displayed update prompts. These prompts looked like errors, but they weren’t.

• Why does my code look exactly like the projection but fail to run? There are four spelling mistakes (`soket`, `io.socket`, `part 3000`). Typing `node` on its own also takes me to the Node > prompt, where I remain until I press Ctrl+C to exit.

• Does this allow me to connect with my partner? Not quite. Today’s build only includes the middleware and walkie-talkie functionality. Still missing: a browser sending a signal, the server broadcasting it, and another browser receiving it; in addition, room functionality and online deployment are required. The three layers of Project 1 are: p5 handles drawing, socket.io handles transmission, and ml5 handles gesture recognition.
conclusion_future_work: This week’s reading assignment consists of the first few chapters of Flusser [8] and the p5.js tutorial. Next Tuesday (28 October), each group will present their Project 1 proposal to Boyd, covering the concept, structure and the new narrative layer. Tasks for this weekend: first, write the opening remarks in Chinese, then rewrite them in English; sketch out six gestures; and practise connecting two laptops to the p5 server folder. My partner was absent on Friday, so I am sending him the server folder along with a brief explanation of what each line of code does.
